Lesson 1 · what a call actually costs

Every function call pushes a context

const app = 'rasmi'

function outer() {
  const user = 'ahmed'
  function inner() {
    const page = 2
    return [app, user, page]
  }
  return inner()
}
inner()page · [[Environment]] → outer
outer()user · [[Environment]] → global
globalapp · [[Environment]] → null
Per call: an environment record, plus a pointer to where the function was defined. That pointer is the scope chain — set at definition, not at call.
MODULE 03 · VIDEO 1
04 / 27
Lesson 1 · proof, in six lines

Lexical, not dynamic

const label = 'module'

function read() { return label }

function caller() {
  const label = 'caller'
  return read()
}

caller()   // → 'module'
read was written next to the module-level label, so that is the one it sees — no matter who calls it, or from where.

Three consequences worth naming

  • A missing binding walks up, never sidewaysand ends in a ReferenceError, not undefined
  • let and const exist in the record from the first linebut reading before the declaration throws — that is the temporal dead zone, not "not hoisted"
  • var is initialised to undefined insteadwhich is why the two behave differently in a loop

The definition that survives an interview

A function plus the environment it was born in

function counter() {
  let n = 0                 // lives in counter's record
  return () => ++n           // holds a reference to it
}

const a = counter(), b = counter()
a(); a()   // 1, 2
b()        // 1  — a separate record
The frame popped; the environment record did not die, because the returned function still points at it.

The classic, and why it changed

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i))
// 3, 3, 3 — one binding, shared

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++)
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i))
// 0, 1, 2 — a fresh binding per iteration

Where you already rely on it

Three shapes, one mechanism

Private state

A value only the returned functions can reach. No #private, no convention, no way to poke at it from outside.

const store = makeStore()
store.get()  // ✓
store.state  // undefined

Remembered arguments

Every partial application, every curried handler, every onClick={() => remove(id)} in a list is a closure over id.

const on = (id) =>
  () => remove(id)

A slot between calls

The timer handle in debounce, the last-run stamp in throttle, the cache in memoize. Lesson 9 is three closures and nothing else.

let t
return (...args) => {
  clearTimeout(t); ...
}
If you can explain the counter on the last slide, you can already write debounce. Lesson 9 adds the timer, not the idea.

07 / 27
The other edge of the same knife

What the closure keeps alive

The cost

An environment record is reachable as long as any function that closes over it is reachable. One surviving callback can hold a 4MB response, a detached DOM node, or the whole component tree it was created in.

function attach(node) {
  const big = hugePayload()
  node.onclick = () => log('hi')
  // `big` is in the same record —
  // engines may keep it alive
}

The discipline

Keep the closed-over surface small: capture the one value you need, not the object it came from. Null out handles you own. Return an unsubscribe from anything that subscribes.

// capture the id, not the record
const { id } = job
return () => open(id)
"A memory leak is a closure that remembered something nobody asked it to." Lesson 8 measures exactly this.

Read the call, not the definition

Four rules, checked in this order

function who() { return this }

who()                      // 1 · default
obj.who()                  // 2 · implicit
who.call(other)            // 3 · explicit
new Who()                  // 4 · construction
Arrows are not on this list: no this of their own, read from the enclosing scope. Bad methods, perfect callbacks.
this → undefined

09 / 27
The bug you have shipped at least once

A method passed by reference loses its dot

class Search {
  query = ''
  handle(e) { this.query = e.target.value }
}

const s = new Search()
input.addEventListener('input', s.handle)
// TypeError: Cannot set property of undefined
// the listener calls handle() — no dot, no this

Three fixes, in order of preference

  • Class field with an arrowhandle = (e) => { this.query = … } — bound at construction, one per instance
  • Wrap at the call siteel.addEventListener('input', e => s.handle(e)) — nothing to remember later
  • .bind(this) in the constructorworks, but you must remember the same reference to remove the listener
Never .bind() inline in a render — a new function identity every render breaks removal, memoisation and every equality check downstream.

Lesson 4 · delegation, without classes

Inheritance without classes or constructors

// Pure prototypal delegation
const protoUser = {
  login() { return `${this.name} logged in`; },
  hasAccess() { return this.role === 'admin'; }
};

// Create new object delegating to protoUser
const userA = Object.create(protoUser);
userA.name = 'Layla';
userA.role = 'editor';

console.log(userA.login()); // "Layla logged in"
console.log(userA.hasOwnProperty('login')); // false!
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(userA) === protoUser); // true

Differential Inheritance

userA only stores what makes it unique (name, role). All behavioral methods reside on protoUser.

The Prototype Pattern: new objects by delegating to an archetype, not by invoking a constructor.

Lesson 4 · what class is hiding

What 'class' is actually hiding

ES6 Class Syntax
class User {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }
  login() {
    return this.name;
  }
}
What V8 Actually Executes
function User(name) {
  this.name = name;
}
User.prototype.login = function() {
  return this.name;
};
// User is still a function!
console.log(typeof User); // 'function'
"Does JavaScript have true classes?" No — sugar over constructor functions and prototype chains. The runtime model is prototypal.

Lesson 4 · intercepting the object model

Intercept and control property access

A Proxy wraps a target object and intercepts operations using handler traps.
const user = { name: 'Omar', age: 28 };

const userProxy = new Proxy(user, {
  get(target, prop, receiver) {
    console.log(`Accessed ${String(prop)}`);
    return Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver);
  },
  set(target, prop, value, receiver) {
    if (prop === 'age' && typeof value !== 'number') {
      throw new TypeError('Age must be a number');
    }
    return Reflect.set(target, prop, value, receiver);
  }
});

userProxy.age = 'thirty'; // throws TypeError!

The Core Traps

TrapTriggered By
getReading property (obj.prop)
setWriting property (obj.prop = v)
has'prop' in obj
deletePropertydelete obj.prop
applyCalling function (fn(...args))

Lesson 5 · at runtime

What 'import' actually does at runtime

// counter.js
export let count = 0;
export function inc() { count++; }

// app.js
import { count, inc } from './counter.js';

console.log(count); // 0
inc();
console.log(count); // 1 — live binding reflects update!
// count = 5; // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable

Three Phases of ESM Loading

  • ConstructionParse code into a Static Module Record and resolve dependencies
  • InstantiationAllocate memory locations for all exports & link bindings (no code runs yet!)
  • EvaluationExecute module code and fill the allocated memory slots with real values
CommonJS copies values; ESM links live bindings — which is why circular imports resolve there and half-build in CommonJS.

Lesson 5 · why that bites on the server

Why senior engineers call it an anti-pattern

1 · Test Cross-Pollution

Global state lingers across test files. Test B fails because Test A mutated the singleton. Resetting state requires manual tear-down in afterEach.

2 · Hidden Dependencies

Components import the singleton directly instead of receiving it via props or DI. You cannot swap a mock client or a different config without monkey-patching.

3 · The SSR Request Leak

In Next.js / Node server runtimes, module singletons are shared across all concurrent HTTP requests. User A's session or cart leaks to User B!

In SSR and React, Singletons are a memory and security liability. Use React Provider or request-scoped Dependency Injection instead.

16 / 27
The same fetch, written three ways

await is a .then you can read top to bottom

// 1 · callbacks — one nesting level per step,
//     and an error check inside each one

// 2 · promises — flat, composable
getUser(id)
  .then(getJobs)
  .then(render)
  .catch(fail)
// 3 · async/await — the same chain
async function show(id) {
  try {
    const user = await getUser(id)
    const jobs = await getJobs(user)
    render(jobs)
  } catch (e) { fail(e) }
}
Dependent awaits belong in series. Independent ones cost both round trips for nothing — await Promise.all([getJobs(), getFilters()]).

The four combinators, and when each is right

Pick by what failure should mean

Promise.allAll fulfil — or the first rejects
Promise.allSettledEvery promise finishes, whatever the outcome
Promise.raceThe first to settle, either way
Promise.anyThe first to fulfil; rejects only if all do
fast120ms · rejects
slow900ms · fulfils
middle500ms · fulfils
Pick a combinator, then run it.
Promise.all rejects on the first failure but cancels nothing — watch the other two keep going.

18 / 27
fetch · the rejection that never comes

A 500 is a successful request

// looks safe, ships a broken screen
const res = await fetch('/api/jobs')
const jobs = await res.json()
// 404 → res.ok false → json() throws
// "Unexpected token < in JSON"
fetch rejects only on a network failure — DNS, offline, CORS, abort. Any HTTP status your server sends, 200 to 599, is a fulfilled promise.
async function getJSON(url, opts) {
  const res = await fetch(url, opts)
  if (!res.ok) {
    throw new HttpError(res.status, url)
  }
  return res.json()
}
One wrapper, used everywhere. Now a 404 and a dropped connection arrive at the same catch, carrying enough information to tell them apart.
It bites the other way too: res.json() on a 204 throws, and an abort rejects with an AbortError you want to swallow.

Where to catch, and what to say

Three boundaries, three jobs

At the call

Only if you can do something: retry, fall back to cache, use a default. Catching to console.log and continuing is how a broken screen becomes a silent one.

At the feature

One boundary per screen — an error boundary in React, one catch per route loader. It owns the user-facing message and the retry button.

At the top

unhandledrejection and window.onerror feed your telemetry. This is a smoke alarm, not a fire extinguisher — anything reaching here is a bug in the two above.

"A try only catches a throw in the same turn of the loop — so I await, wrap fetch so a status becomes a rejection, and give each feature one boundary."

Lesson 8 · the leak your SPA has right now

The #1 memory leak in single-page applications

Forgetting to unsubscribe holds entire component trees hostage from Garbage Collection.

The Retained Closure Graph

When component <UserProfile /> calls eventBus.on('theme', onThemeChange), the event bus keeps a pointer to onThemeChange.

onThemeChange's closure scope references the component's state, props, and DOM nodes. When the user navigates away, the entire tree cannot be collected!

The Three Defenses

  • Always teardown in cleanupuseEffect(() => eventBus.on(..., fn), [])
  • AbortController SignalPass { signal } to native addEventListener
  • WeakRef & FinalizationRegistryFor advanced frameworks: allow GC to reclaim dead listeners

Lesson 8 · the two weak collections

When the key should own the lifetime

// strong: this Map is a root, forever
const meta = new Map()
meta.set(node, { seen: true })
node.remove()
// node is detached — and still alive,
// because meta holds it as a key

// weak: the entry dies with the node
const meta = new WeakMap()
meta.set(node, { seen: true })
node.remove()
// nothing else references node → both collected
Holds its keyIterable / sized
Map / SetYes — stronglyYes
WeakMap / WeakSetNoNo — and that is the price
WeakMap when you are annotating something you do not own. Map when the cache is the owner — and then bound it.
WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry run at the collector's convenience — name them in an interview, avoid them in app code.

debounce(fn, wait)

24 / 27
Live coding · from an empty file

Both, in nine lines each

function debounce(fn, wait = 300) {
  let t                        // the closure slot
  function debounced(...args) {
    clearTimeout(t)
    t = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), wait)
  }
  debounced.cancel = () => clearTimeout(t)
  return debounced
}
Three details that get marked: ...args forwarded, fn.apply(this, …) so a method keeps its receiver, and a cancel for teardown.
function throttle(fn, limit = 300) {
  let last = 0, timer
  return function (...args) {
    const now = Date.now()
    const left = limit - (now - last)
    if (left <= 0) {
      last = now; fn.apply(this, args)      // leading
    } else if (!timer) {                   // trailing
      timer = setTimeout(() => {
        last = Date.now(); timer = null
        fn.apply(this, args)
      }, left)
    }
  }
}
Not an arrow at the top level: debounce(obj.method) would silently lose its receiver. Lesson 3, cashed in.

Lesson 10 · the distinction they probe

Observer vs Publish-Subscribe: The crucial difference

Observer Pattern

Direct Coupling: The Subject directly maintains a collection of Observer references. When something happens, the Subject iterates through them and calls their update method.

Usually synchronous and lives in the same memory context.

Publish / Subscribe (Pub-Sub)

Zero Coupling: Publishers and Subscribers never know each other exists. They communicate through a third-party Event Broker or Event Bus.

Can easily bridge asynchronous boundaries, WebSockets, or separate micro-frontends.

"Is Pub-Sub just Observer?" — Pub-Sub adds a broker, so publisher and subscriber never know each other.

Say this in the interview

Four sentences that win the architecture question

1 · Static imports for tree-shaking, dynamic import() for route splitting.

2 · No module singletons in SSR — they leak state across concurrent requests.

3 · Proxy with Reflect at boundaries, never in a hot loop.

4 · Thousands of records: prototype delegation, not closures per instance.
